Which number are you watching next, CPI or the dollar?

hits.draft_en:
Google is building custody tech for banks holding crypto.

Useful for institutions.
But notice what it's selling:
a safer way to let someone else hold your keys.

For a $BTC spot holder the options are still the same:
- exchange: easy, counterparty risk
- custodian (bank, Google stack): regulated, still an IOU
- self-custody: your keys, your responsibility

None is free of risk. Pick the one whose failure mode you understand.

Which one do you use today, and why?
Save this if you're still deciding.
hits.draft_quote_en:
Better custody for banks is good news for banks.

The question for holders: does this make it easier to withdraw to your own keys, or easier to never leave the custodian? Those are very different outcomes for $BTC.

hits.why_chosen: Top fresh post from the account with 100+ replies; clear room for a custody vs. self-custody angle.

Three Bitcoin Core vulnerabilities disclosed, one lets malicious peers crash some nodes, per BitcoinNews.com.

If you run a node, the practical part:
- check which versions are affected
- update from the official release
- verify the signatures before installing

Public disclosure after a fix is how open source is supposed to work.
The risk is people who never update.

When did you last update your node?
Save this for your next node maintenance.

hits.name: Jack Mallers
hits.text:
My dad always said: for everything in life, even gold, more demand finds more supply.

He was right. Until bitcoin. https://t.co/39k7B5kICT
hits.hook: My dad always said: for everything in life, even gold, more demand finds more supply.
hits.story: More demand, more supply, except bitcoin
hits.draft_en:
'More demand finds more supply. Even gold. Until bitcoin.'

The supply side is true: 21M cap, issuance set in code.

But fixed supply doesn't fix the price.
With supply fixed, demand swings hit price directly.
That's part of why $BTC drawdowns are so deep.

Scarcity is the feature. Volatility is the cost.
Are you sized for both?
If it was useful, a repost helps more people see it.
hits.draft_quote_en:
Fixed supply, agreed.

The other side: when demand drops, supply can't adjust either. Fixed supply means demand alone sets the price, both ways.
hits.video_tip: Gold mine output rising vs. a flat 21M line, then a price line swinging; 12s.
hits.reply_angle: Add the missing half: inelastic supply means demand shocks go straight to price; point to past $BTC drawdowns as the cost of scarcity.
hits.why_chosen: Clean scarcity claim with good saves; room to add the volatility side.

'A dip below the 50-week average isn't bearish. Same pattern in 2023, then +49% in 30 days.'

Maybe. But that's one example.

Before trusting a setup:
- how many times did it happen?
- what was the median result, not the best one?
- how many times did it fail?

One chart is a story. A sample is evidence.

Anyone have the full list of 50-week MA breaks for $BTC?
Save this for the next 'same pattern as' chart.
hits.draft_quote_en:
One instance from 2023 isn't a base rate.

How many times has $BTC closed below the 50-week MA after a rally, and what did the next 30 days look like in each case? The median would say more than the best one.

hits.reply_angle: Turn the n=1 claim into a base rate: list every $BTC close below the 50-week MA after a rally and check the median 30-day return (backtest to run, don't quote a figure).

hits.text: The most important revolution of our lifetime is separating money from the state.

hits.story: Separating money from the state
hits.draft_en:
"Separate money from the state" sounds simple.

In practice it means three things:
- no one can print more $BTC
- no one can freeze coins you hold yourself
- no one can block a valid transaction

The last two only apply if you hold your own keys.
On an exchange you still have a counterparty.

Which of the three matters most to you?
Want me to go deeper on any part?
hits.draft_quote_en:
Agreed on the protocol side: fixed supply, no one can print more.

But the separation only reaches you if you hold your own keys. Coins on an exchange are still a claim inside the old system.
